passages.source_text: ἀλλὰ διὰ τί (φησίν) ὁ ἀνὴρ ἐὰν ἀγνοῇ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γυναῖκα μοιχευομένην, οὐ ζηλοῖ, οὐ θυμοῦται, οὐ θορυβεῖ, οὐ πολεμεῖ; οὕτως οὐκ ἔστιν τῇ φύσει τὰ τοιαῦτα κακά, ἀλλὰ ἡ ἄλογος ἀνθρώπων δόκησις ταῦτα δεινοποιεῖ. ἐγὼ δὲ φημὶ ὅτι κἂν μὴ τὰ δεινὰ ταῦτα συμβαίνῃ, ἐνδέχεται συνηθείᾳ τῇ πρὸς τὸν μοιχὸν ἢ τὸν ἄνδρα ἀπολιπεῖν ἢ καὶ συνοικοῦσαν ἐπιβουλεῦσαι ἢ τὰ τοῦ ἀνδρὸς κόπῳ πεπορισμένα τῷ μοιχῷ παρασχεῖν καὶ ἀποδημοῦντος τοῦ ἀνδρὸς συλλαβοῦσαν ἐκ τοῦ μοιχοῦ διὰ τὸ αἰδεῖσθαι τὸν ἔλεγχον τὸ κατὰ γαστρὸς φθεῖραι θελῆσαι καὶ γενέσθαι τεκνοκτόνον ἢ καὶ φθείρουσαν συνφθαρῆναι· εἰ δὲ συνόντος τοῦ ἀνδρὸς ἐκ μοιχοῦ συλλαβοῦσα τέκοι, ἀνατραφεὶς ὁ -παῖς τὸν μὲν πατέρα ἀγνοεῖ, τὸν δὲ οὐκ ὄντα νομίζει, καὶ οὕτως ὁ μὴ πατὴρ τελευτῶν ἀλλοτρίῳ παιδὶ τὸν ἑαυτοῦ καταλείπει βίον. πόσα δὲ καὶ ἄλλα κακὰ ἐκ τῆς μοιχείας φυσικῶς ἀνακύπτειν φιλεῖ. καὶ οὐκ ἴσμεν τὰ κρύφια τῶν κακῶν. ὥσπερ γὰρ ὁ λυσσῶν κύων τούτους ἀναιρεῖ ὧνπερ ἂν ψαύσῃ, τῆς ἀφανεστάτης λύσσης μεταδιδούς, οὕτως καὶ τῆς μοιχείας τὸ κρύφιον κακόν, κἂν ἀγνοῆται, τῆς διαδοχῆς τὴν ἐκκοπὴν ἐξεργάζεται.

ἀλλὰ τοῦτο μὲν νῦν ἡμῖν παραλελείφθω, ἐκεῖνο δὲ ἅπαντες ἴσμεν ὡς ἐπίπαν ἐπὶ τούτῳ τοὺς ἄνδρας ἀνεπισχέτως δυσχεραίνοντας πολέμους τε ἐπὶ τούτῳ ἐγηγερμένους καὶ οἴκων γενομένας ἀνατροπὰς καὶ πόλεων ἁλώσεις καὶ ἄλλα μυρία. διὰ τοῦτο ἐγὼ τῷ ἁγίῳ τῶν Ἰουδαίων θεῷ καὶ νόμῳ προσέφυγον, ἀποδεδωκὼς τὴν πίστιν ἀσφαλεῖ τῇ κρίσει ὅτι ἐκ τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ δικαίας κρίσεως καὶ νόμος ὥρισται καὶ ἡ ψυχὴ πάντως τὸ κατ’ ἀξίαν ὧν ἔπραξεν ὁπουδήποτε ἀπολαμβάνει.

ταῦτά μου εἰπόντος ὁ Ἀππίων ἐπήνεγκεν τῷ λόγῳ Τί γάρ; οὐχὶ καὶ οἱ Ἑλλήνων (ἔφη) νόμοι τὰ φαῦλα ἀπαγορεύουσιν καὶ τοὺς μοιχοὺς κολάζουσιν; κἀγὼ ἔφην Οὐκοῦν οἱ Ἑλλήνων θεοὶ τὰ ἐναντία τοῖς νόμοις πράξαντες κόλασιν ὀφείλουσιν. πῶς· δὲ καὶ σωφρονίζειν ἐμαυτὸν δυνήσομαι ὑπολαμβάνων ὅτι οἱ θεοὶ αὐτοὶ πρῶτοι ἅμα τῇ μοιχείᾳ τὰ χαλεπὰ πάντα διεπράξαντο καὶ δίκην οὐ δεδώκασιν, ταύτῃ μᾶλλον ὀφείλοντες διδόναι ὡς μὴ δουλεύοντες ἐπιθυμίᾳ; εἰ δὲ ὑπέκειντο, πῶς ἦσαν θεοί; καὶ ὁ Ἀππίων Ἔστωσαν ἡμῖν σκοποὶ μηκέτι θεοί, ἀλλ’ οἱ δικασταὶ εἰς οὓς ἀφορῶντες φοβηθησόμεθα ἁμαρτάνειν. κἀγὼ ἔφην Οὐκ ἔσθ’ ὅμοιον, ὦ Ἀππίων· ὁ μὲν γὰρ πρὸς ἄνθρωπον ἔχων τὸν σκοπὸν ἐλπίδι τοῦ λαθεῖν τολμήσει ἁμαρτάνειν, ὁ δὲ θεὸν παντεπόπτην τῇ ἑαυτοῦ ψυχῇ ὁρισάμενος, εἰδὼς αὐτὸν λαθεῖν μὴ δύνασθαι καὶ τὸ λάθρα ἁμαρτεῖν παραιτήσεται.

ταῦτα ὁ Ἀππίων ἀκούσας ἔφη Ἤδειν ἐξότε ἤκουσα Ἰουδαίοις σε προσομιλοῦντα, ἠλλοιῶσθαι τὴν γνώμην. καλῶς γὰρ εἴρηταί τινι „φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρηστὰ ὁμιλίαι κακαί“. κἀγὼ ἔφην Οὐκοῦν ἐπανορθοῦσιν ἤθη ἄχρηστα ὁμιλίαι καλαί. καὶ ὁ Ἀππίων ἔφη Σήμερον πεπληροφορήμην τὴν σὴν ἐπιγνῶναι ἔνστασιν, διὸ σοὶ πρώτῳ εἰπεῖν συνεχωρήσαμεν· αὔριον δὲ (ἐνταῦθα, εἴ σοι φίλον ἐστίν) ἐπὶ τῶν αὐτῶν φίλων συνελθόντων ἀποδείξω ὅτι οἱ θεοὶ ἡμῶν οὔτε μοιχοὶ ὄντες τυγχάνουσιν οὔτε φονεῖς οὔτε παίδων φθορεῖς, οὐχ ἀδελφαῖς ἢ θυγατράσιν πλησιάσαντες, ἀλλ’ οἱ ἀρχαῖοι τὰ μυστήρια μόνους τοὺς φιλομαθεῖς εἰδέναι θέλοντες μύθοις οἷς εἴρηκας αὐτὰ προεκάλυψαν. Ζῆνα γὰρ τὴν ζέουσαν οὐσίαν εἶναι φυσιολογοῦσιν, Κρόνον δὲ τὸν χρόνον καὶ Ῥέαν τὴν ἀεὶ ῥέουσαν τοῦ ὕδατος φύσιν. πλὴν ὡς ὑπεσχόμην, αὔριον τὸ καθ’ ἕκαστον εἶδος ἕωθεν ὑμῖν συνελθοῦσιν ἀλληγορήσας τὴν τῶν ὄντων ἀλήθειαν ἐκφανῶ. κἀγὼ πρὸς ταῦτα ἔφην Αὔριον ὡς ὑπέσχου, οὕτως ποίησον· ἤδη δὲ ἐντεῦθεν καὶ πρὸς αὐτὰ ἃ μέλλεις λέγειν, ἄκουσον.

αἱ τῶν θεῶν πράξεις εἰ μὲν ἀγαθαὶ οὖσαι κακοῖς μύθοις προεκαλύφθησαν, πολλὴ τοῦ σκεπάσαντος δείκνυται κακία, ὅτι τὰ σεμνὰ ἀπέκρυψεν κακοῖς διηγήμασιν, ἵνα μήτις αὐτῶν ζηλωτὴς γένηται· εἰ δὲ ἀληθῶς ἀσεβῆ διεπράξαντο, ἐχρῆν τοὐναντίον ἀγαθοῖς αὐτὰ ἐπισκέπειν, ἵνα μὴ οἱ ἄνθρωποι ὡς εἰς κρείττονας ἀφορώντες, ἁμαρτάνειν ἐπιχειρῶσιν ἐκείνοις παραπλήσια. ταῦτά μου εἰπόντος οἱ παρόντες φανεροὶ ἦσαν ἀρχὴν λαμβάνοντες τῆς πρὸς τοὺς ὑπ’ ἐμοῦ λεχθέντας λόγους · ἀγάπης. καὶ γὰρ συνεχῶς καὶ ἐσπουδασμένως ἀξιοῦντες πάντως με τῇ ὑστεραίᾳ ἐλθεῖν ἀπηλλάγησαν.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

passages.text: “But why,” he says, “if a man does not know that his own wife is committing adultery, does he not become jealous, grow angry, cause an uproar, or wage war? Thus such things are not evils by nature; rather, irrational human opinion makes them terrible.” But I say that, even if these terrible things do not happen, it is possible for the wife, through her intimacy with the adulterer, either to abandon her husband, or, even while living with him, to plot against him, or to give the adulterer what her husband acquired through toil. And while her husband is away, she may conceive by the adulterer and, because she is ashamed of being exposed, wish to destroy what is in her womb and become a child-killer, or, while destroying it, perish along with it. But if she conceives by an adulterer while her husband is living with her and then gives birth, the child, once reared, does not know his father but takes the man who is not his father to be his father. And so, when the man who is not his father dies, he leaves his own estate to someone else’s child. And how many other evils naturally tend to spring from adultery! We do not know the hidden things belonging to these evils. For just as a rabid dog kills those whom it touches by transmitting its utterly unseen rabies, so also the hidden evil of adultery, even when it remains unknown, brings about the severing of succession.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κἂν μὴ τὰ δεινὰ ταῦτα συμβαίνῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: even if these terrible things do not happen
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase may refer particularly to the husband’s jealousy, anger, uproar, and conflict, or more generally to the harmful consequences just discussed; the English preserves that breadth.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through her intimacy with the adulterer
lexical_decisions.rationale: συνήθεια can denote familiarity, association, or intimacy; the adulterous context supports “intimacy,” while the wife remains the understood subject of the following infinitives.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to destroy what is in her womb
lexical_decisions.rationale: The idiom τὸ κατὰ γαστρός denotes what is in the womb. “Destroy” preserves φθείρω without replacing the author’s wording with a modern technical term.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he leaves his own estate
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here βίος most naturally means one’s means of living or property left at death, rather than biological life; “livelihood” or “possessions” are possible alternatives.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the severing of succession
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαδοχή may denote succession, inheritance, or continuation of a family line. The context of misidentified paternity and inheritance favors “succession” while leaving the precise dimension open.

source_issues.issue: The printed form has unassimilated συν- before φ. It is intelligible as an orthographic form of the compound meaning “to be destroyed together,” so no content is uncertain.
The prefixed hyphen is present in the supplied image-checked reading but has no evident syntactic or morphological function. It is treated as a typographical feature rather than as part of the noun.

passages.text: But let that now be passed over by us. This, however, we all know: as a rule, men are uncontrollably indignant over it; wars have been stirred up over it, households have been overthrown, cities have been captured, and countless other things have occurred. For this reason I took refuge with the Jews’ holy God and their law, having placed my confidence in the firm judgment that, from God’s just judgment, both law has been laid down and the soul, wherever it may be, certainly receives what its deeds deserve.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as a rule
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression indicates what happens generally or for the most part, not an exceptionless claim.

lexical_decisions.chosen: are uncontrollably indignant
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀνεπισχέτως conveys lack of restraint, while δυσχεραίνω can mean to be displeased, distressed, or indignant; the ensuing wars and destruction support the stronger contextual wording.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀποδεδωκὼς τὴν πίστιν ἀσφαλεῖ τῇ κρίσει
lexical_decisions.chosen: having placed my confidence in the firm judgment
lexical_decisions.rationale: πίστις here denotes confidence or credence given to a conclusion. An alternative is “having entrusted my faith to the sure judgment,” but that can suggest a more technical religious use than the construction requires.

lexical_decisions.chosen: what its deeds deserve
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally, the soul receives “what is according to the worth of the things it did”; the rendering expresses proportionate recompense without specifying reward or punishment beyond the Greek.

passages.text:
After I said this, Appion added to the argument, saying, “What then? Do not the laws of the Greeks also forbid base acts and punish adulterers?”

I said, “Then the gods of the Greeks, since they have acted contrary to the laws, owe a penalty. Moreover, how will I be able to discipline myself if I suppose that the gods themselves were the first to commit every grievous act along with adultery and have paid no penalty, although they owe it all the more for this very reason, since they are not enslaved to desire? But if they were subject to it, how could they be gods?”

Appion said, “Then let our objects of attention no longer be gods, but the judges; with our eyes on them, we will be afraid to sin.”

I replied, “The cases are not alike, Appion. A person who keeps a human being in view will dare to sin in the hope of escaping notice. But one who has settled in his own mind that God sees everything, knowing that he cannot escape God’s notice, will refrain even from sinning in secret.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: added to the argument
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression means to bring or add something to the ongoing discourse; “responded to the argument” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they owe it all the more for this very reason
lexical_decisions.rationale: ταύτῃ points forward to their not being enslaved to desire: freedom from compulsion makes the gods, on the speaker’s reasoning, more accountable.

lexical_decisions.chosen: let our objects of attention be
lexical_decisions.rationale: σκοποί can mean goals, marks, or objects kept in view. The following εἰς οὓς ἀφορῶντες supports the visual and exemplary sense rather than “goals” alone.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: θεὸν παντεπόπτην τῇ ἑαυτοῦ ψυχῇ ὁρισάμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: one who has settled in his own mind that God sees everything
lexical_decisions.rationale: The construction can be rendered more formally as “one who has defined God in his soul as all-seeing.” The chosen wording gives a defensible modern English expression of the internal conviction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: will refrain even from sinning in secret
lexical_decisions.rationale: παραιτέομαι here means to decline, avoid, or refrain from an action; καί adds the force “even” in context.

source_issues.issue: The image-checked edition prints a middle dot between πῶς and the postpositive δέ. That punctuation syntactically interrupts what is otherwise a coherent question, so the translation reads the words together without changing them.

passages.text:
When Appion heard this, he said, “Ever since I heard that you were associating with Jews, I knew that your outlook had changed. For someone has aptly said, ‘Bad associations corrupt good character.’”

I replied, “Then good associations correct worthless character.”

Appion said, “Today I have become fully assured that I understand your position, and that is why we allowed you to speak first. But tomorrow—here, if it pleases you—when the same friends have assembled, I will demonstrate that our gods are neither adulterers nor murderers nor destroyers of children, and that they did not have sexual relations with sisters or daughters. Rather, the ancients, wishing only lovers of learning to know the mysteries, veiled them in myths of the kind you have described. For in their account of nature they say that Zeus is the boiling substance, Cronus is time, and Rhea is the ever-flowing nature of water. Nevertheless, as I promised, tomorrow at dawn, when you have assembled, I will interpret each particular form allegorically and reveal to you the truth about what exists.”

In response I said, “Tomorrow do just as you have promised. But now, beginning from this point, listen also to what bears on the very things you are going to say.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: your outlook had changed
lexical_decisions.rationale: γνώμη can denote mind, judgment, opinion, or outlook. The passive ἠλλοιῶσθαι indicates that it had been altered.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Bad associations corrupt good character
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὁμιλίαι denotes associations or company, and ἤθη denotes habits, morals, or character. The wording preserves the maxim and its reversal in the next sentence without importing a familiar scriptural formulation as controlling text.

lexical_decisions.chosen: that I understand your position
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔνστασις can mean an objection, position, contention, or line of argument. “Position” fits Appion’s claim that he now understands Clement’s case; “objection” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: destroyers of children
lexical_decisions.rationale: φθορεύς can denote a destroyer or corrupter. In a list with adultery and murder and in the context of myths about the gods, “destroyers” is the more direct choice, though “corrupters of children” is lexically possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they did not have sexual relations with sisters or daughters
lexical_decisions.rationale: πλησιάζω literally means to approach or associate closely, but with these dative objects and the surrounding accusations of sexual misconduct it has a sexual sense.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ζῆνα γὰρ τὴν ζέουσαν οὐσίαν εἶναι φυσιολογοῦσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: in their account of nature they say that Zeus is the boiling substance
lexical_decisions.rationale: φυσιολογοῦσιν introduces a natural-philosophical explanation. The Greek also makes an etymological sound association between Ζῆνα and ζέουσαν that cannot be reproduced naturally in English.

lexical_decisions.chosen: each particular form
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase may refer to each divine figure, each mythic form, or each individual feature of the allegory. “Form” preserves the expression without selecting one referent too narrowly.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐντεῦθεν καὶ πρὸς αὐτὰ ἃ μέλλεις λέγειν, ἄκουσον
lexical_decisions.chosen: beginning from this point, listen also to what bears on the very things you are going to say
lexical_decisions.rationale: The Greek elliptically commands Appion to hear something directed toward or bearing upon his forthcoming claims. “A reply to” is another possible way to supply the English relation.

passages.text:
If the deeds of the gods, though good, were veiled in evil myths, great wickedness is revealed in the one who covered them, because he hid honorable things beneath evil narratives so that no one might become an imitator of them. But if they truly committed impious acts, those acts should instead have been covered with good narratives, so that people, looking up to them as their superiors, would not attempt sins like theirs.

After I said this, those present were plainly beginning to feel love for the arguments I had made. Indeed, after repeatedly and earnestly urging me to come without fail on the following day, they departed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: great wickedness is revealed in the one who covered them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive identifies the person responsible for concealing the deeds; “is demonstrated on the part of the one who covered them” is a more formal alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: honorable things
lexical_decisions.rationale: σεμνός can mean venerable, august, solemn, or honorable. Here it describes supposedly good divine deeds that would merit imitation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those acts should instead have been covered with good narratives
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπισκέπειν is understood here in the sense of covering over, corresponding to the earlier language of veiling. The substantival ἀγαθοῖς takes its contextual content from the preceding “myths” and “narratives.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: looking up to them as their superiors
lexical_decisions.rationale: κρείττονας may mean those who are better, stronger, or superior. The gods function here as supposedly higher examples whom humans observe and imitate.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀρχὴν λαμβάνοντες τῆς πρὸς τοὺς ὑπ’ ἐμοῦ λεχθέντας λόγους · ἀγάπης
lexical_decisions.chosen: beginning to feel love for the arguments I had made
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀρχὴν λαμβάνειν with the genitive means to make a beginning of something. λόγοι may be words, statements, or arguments; the argumentative setting favors “arguments,” while the printed middle dot is treated as editorial punctuation that does not prevent ἀγάπης from completing the construction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: me to come without fail on the following day
lexical_decisions.rationale: πάντως expresses insistence that the visit occur in any event or by all means.

source_issues.source_quote: τῆς πρὸς τοὺς ὑπ’ ἐμοῦ λεχθέντας λόγους · ἀγάπης
source_issues.issue: The image-checked edition prints a middle dot between λόγους and ἀγάπης, although the surrounding words support the continuous genitive construction “love for the arguments spoken by me.” The translation retains that defensible syntax while disclosing the printed punctuation.
source_issues.proposed_reading: τῆς πρὸς τοὺς ὑπ’ ἐμοῦ λεχθέντας λόγους ἀγάπης

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
